pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 10–11 — recognise that a digit represents 10× the place to its right and 1/10 the place to its left (the ×10/÷10 place-value relationship, now extended in BOTH directions across the decimal point).
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics): Y5 'recognise the place value of each digit in numbers with up to 3 decimal places' and multiply/divide by 10/100/1000; the reciprocal ÷10 direction underpins Y6 decimal work.
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 5.NBT.A.1 — 'Recognize that in a multi-digit number, a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as it represents in the place to its right and 1/10 of what it represents in the place to its left.'
• Operational details: Treat place value as a single self-similar structure that continues seamlessly through the decimal point — each step left is unitising (×10), each step right is partitioning (÷10). Contrast digits of equal face value in different places (the 4 in 0.4 vs 0.04 vs 4000) so the child articulates the multiplicative, not additive, gap. Use a Gattegno/place-value chart where a digit physically slides between columns and its value recomputes.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 10): 'The 4 in 0.4 is ten times the 4 in ___.' Tier B: 'Explain why the 6 in 6000 is a million times the 6 in 0.006.' Tier C: 'A digit moves two places right — what happens to its value and why?'
bestPractices: Present place value as one continuous ×10/÷10 chain that runs unbroken through the decimal point — do not teach whole-number and decimal place value as separate systems
Use a Gattegno chart or place-value slider so a digit physically moves between columns and its value visibly recomputes (×10 left, ÷10 right)
Contrast the SAME face-value digit sitting in different places (4 in 4000 vs 0.4 vs 0.04) and require a multiplicative statement ('ten times', 'one tenth of'), never 'bigger/smaller'
Anchor the ÷10 direction in concrete partitioning — one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth — before abstracting to the rule
Vary the non-example: ask why moving a place is NOT 'add a zero' when decimals are involved, exposing the multiplicative meaning
keyRepresentations: Gattegno / place-value chart (digit slides between columns, value scales ×10 or ÷10)
Place-value chart spanning millions to thousandths with the decimal point fixed and digits mobile
Arrow/relationship cards labelling adjacent columns '×10 →' and '← ÷10'
Base-ten / Dienes extended to decimal flats-longs-units where the 'one' can be reassigned
commonMisconceptions: Believing 'moving a place left just adds a zero' — a rule that breaks for decimals (0.4 → 4, not 0.40)
Treating the decimal point as moving rather than the DIGITS moving relative to a fixed point
Thinking the gap between places is additive (0.4 is '0.36 more than' 0.04) rather than multiplicative (ten times)
Assuming longer decimals are always larger, ignoring place value (0.004 seen as bigger than 0.4)
Losing the self-similar structure at the decimal point — seeing tenths as unrelated to ones

learn.summary: For ages 10–11: understand that each place in a number is worth ten times the place to its right and one tenth of the place to its left, and that this ×10/÷10 structure continues unbroken through the decimal point. The core goal is for a learner to state multiplicative relationships ('ten times', 'one tenth of') between the same digit sitting in different places, and to justify them by position rather than by face value or decimal length.

activities.title: Slide the same digit across the places
feedback: If a learner says the two 4s are 'the same because both are 4', redirect to position: the digit is identical but the places differ, so the worth differs — ask them to read each value aloud (four tenths vs four hundredths).
If a learner counts a single move as ÷100 or ÷2, have them count the columns crossed: tenths to hundredths is ONE step, so ÷10; show 0.004 to illustrate what two steps (÷100) would look like.
Reinforce correct multiplicative language: accept 'ten times' / 'one tenth of', and gently reject 'bigger/smaller' or 'add a zero' as the explanation.
activities.rationale: The concept is a transformation of value by place, so performing the move and reading the recomputed value makes the multiplicative gap concrete rather than merely stated. An optional live readout and a proportional magnitude bar that is ten times longer per leftward step can make the multiplicative (not additive) gap visible.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.1: a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as the place to its right and 1/10 of the place to its left.
The Gattegno chart is a canonical representation for building the ×10/÷10 place-value relationship across whole numbers and decimals.
learnerActions: Work on a place-value chart with columns from millions down to thousandths and a fixed decimal point.
Take a single digit, for example a 4, and place it in the tenths column so it reads 0.4.
Move the same 4 one column to the left to read 4, then 40, then 400, then 4000; each move, say aloud 'ten times as much' and write the ×10 relationship.

Before moving right, split one tenth into ten equal parts and check that each part is one hundredth (and one hundredth into ten parts gives thousandths). Then move the same 4 one column to the right from 0.4 to 0.04 to 0.004; each move, say aloud 'one tenth of' and write the ÷10 relationship.
Park the same 4 three columns apart (for example 4000 and 4, or 4 and 0.004 — each three steps, so ×1000) and state how many times larger one is than the other.
Finish the sentence: '0.4 is ten times 0.04; 0.04 is one tenth of 0.4.'
activities.intendedInsight: A digit's worth changes multiplicatively (×10 each step left, ÷10 each step right) according to its place; the decimal point stays fixed while the digit moves, and the same self-similar rule runs through the decimal point.

activities.title: Why isn't it just 'add a zero'?
feedback: If a learner insists 'add a zero' works, show 0.4 → 4: adding a zero gives 0.40, which is still four tenths, not four.
Confirm understanding when the learner states the rule as '×10 when moving left, ÷10 when moving right' and can apply it to a decimal example.
activities.rationale: Directly contrasting a tempting but faulty shortcut with the multiplicative rule surfaces and addresses the common 'add a zero' misconception.
sourceClaims: Y5 requires recognising the place value of each digit in numbers with up to three decimal places and multiplying/dividing by 10, 100 and 1000.
learnerActions: Consider the claim 'moving a digit one place left just adds a zero.'
Test it on whole numbers: 4 → 40 (works) and then on a decimal: 0.4 → 4 (not 0.40).
Explain in your own words why 'add a zero' fails for decimals but ×10 always works.
Write a corrected rule that holds for both whole numbers and decimals.
activities.intendedInsight: The underlying operation is multiply/divide by ten, not a digit-appending trick; 'add a zero' is a surface pattern that breaks for decimals, exposing the multiplicative meaning.

activities.title: Compare across many places and across zero
feedback: If a learner ranks the 4 in 0.04 as larger because it comes 'further along', use the number line to show 0.04 sits close to zero while 0.4 is near halfway.
If a learner cannot bridge 6,000 and 0.006, have them step through the places one at a time, tagging each ×10 (six steps), to reach a million-fold difference.
activities.rationale: Spanning many places and crossing the decimal point counters the 'longer decimal is larger' and 'face value' errors, and a number line makes the shrinking rightward value visible.
sourceClaims: 5.NBT.A.1: a digit in one place represents 10 times as much as the place to its right and 1/10 of the place to its left.
learnerActions: Compare the 6 in 6,000 with the 6 in 0.006: count how many ×10 steps separate the two places (six steps).
State and justify how many times larger the 6 in 6,000 is (6,000 is 0.006 × 1,000,000).
Place 0.4 and 0.04 on a 0–1 number line (0.4 near the middle, 0.04 close to zero) to see the value shrinking to the right.
Explain which stays the same and which changes when a digit moves place — the digit, or its worth.
activities.intendedInsight: The place-value relationship holds across several steps and across the decimal point; value decreases to the right and increases to the left, regardless of decimal length.

activities.title: Explain and defend your reasoning
feedback: A full response states the ten-times / one-tenth relationship, justifies it by positional value, and applies it in both directions and across several places.
A partial response can order the values and say one is smaller but cannot justify the exact ÷10 factor or muddles it; prompt the learner to count places and name the single ×10/÷10 step.
If the learner says one tenth of a tenth is a twentieth or a tenth, have them partition one tenth into ten equal parts to see each part is a hundredth.
activities.rationale: Requiring a justified comparison rather than a memorised ranking discriminates true positional understanding from surface rules, and asking the learner to explain the partitioning met earlier (one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth) checks that the ÷10 direction rests on concrete meaning rather than a memorised rule.
learnerActions: Answer the prompt: 'Look at the 4 in 0.4 and the 4 in 0.04. How do their values compare, and why?'
Answer a deeper probe: 'Why does moving one place to the right divide the value by ten and not some other number?'
Explain, with reasons, why the 6 in 6,000 is a million times the 6 in 0.006.
Anchor the ÷10 direction in partitioning: explain why one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth.
activities.intendedInsight: Being able to justify the exact ÷10/×10 relationship by position — not just order the values — is what demonstrates genuine place-value understanding.

constraints: Present whole-number and decimal place value as ONE continuous ×10/÷10 chain running through the decimal point, not two separate systems.
Require multiplicative language ('ten times', 'one tenth of'); do not accept 'bigger/smaller' or 'add a zero' as the explanation of the relationship.

Recognition-only tasks (for example choosing from multiple options or filling a blank) can consolidate and assess the rule but do not by themselves elicit the learner's own justification; include tasks where the learner states and defends the relationship.

A static annotated chart with reveal cards is a useful reference, but it tells rather than lets the learner perform the slide; treat it as a scaffold, not a substitute for the learner moving a digit and reading the recomputed value.
Partitioning (one tenth of a tenth is a hundredth) should be established concretely before abstracting to the divide-by-ten rule.
Keep worked examples arithmetically exact: columns N apart differ by a factor of 10^N (three columns apart is ×1000, two columns apart is ×100).
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research; sources were NOT re-fetched or re-verified. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Arithmetic/logic self-audit confirmed: 0.4 = 0.04 × 10 and 0.04 = 0.4 ÷ 10; 6,000 vs 0.006 differ by six ×10 steps (a factor of 1,000,000); one tenth of one tenth = one hundredth; three columns apart = ×1000 and two columns apart = ×100. The example pairs 4000 and 4, and 4 and 0.004, are genuinely three steps apart and consistent with the ×1000 framing.

The original claim that a third spatial dimension 'adds nothing' and 'risks implying value scales with physical size' is a catalog preference, not an established pedagogical law; a spatial model could still be used — it is simply not required here.

The original framing that manipulation is 'necessary' while dialogue is merely 'possible' reflects catalog fit ranking, not demonstrated comparative efficacy; both a manipulable chart and a Socratic exchange are retained as legitimate approaches serving different purposes.
CCSS-M 5.NBT.A.1 and the NCETM Gattegno-chart claim were marked unverified in the source row; treat their support as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: Why does moving one place to the right divide the value by ten and not some other number?
How does the 6 in 6,000 compare to the 6 in 0.006 — how many tens apart are they?
If I move the 4 in 0.4 one place LEFT instead, what happens to its value?
What stays the same and what changes when a digit moves place — the digit, or its worth?
assess.correctAnswer: The 4 in 0.04 is worth one-tenth of the 4 in 0.4 (0.04 = 0.4 ÷ 10). A digit one place to the right is worth ten times less, because each place is a tenth of the place to its left.

errorPatterns.pattern: Face value — 'they're the same, both digits are 4', ignoring position.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Confront with place-value counters or a Gattegno chart: slide the 4 from tenths to hundredths and show its worth divides by ten; the digit is the same but its place is not.
errorPatterns.distractor: They're the same — both digits are 4.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child says equal value and justifies by the digit alone.

errorPatterns.pattern: Longer-decimal-is-larger / places grow to the right — thinks the 4 in 0.04 is worth more because it is 'further along'.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Place 0.4 and 0.04 on a 0–1 line (0.4 near halfway, 0.04 close to zero) so the shrinking value to the right is visible.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 in 0.04 is bigger because it comes further along.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child ranks 0.04's 4 as the bigger value.

errorPatterns.pattern: Right direction, wrong factor — says the 0.04 four is a hundredth (or half) of the other, not a tenth.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Count the places moved: tenths→hundredths is ONE step, so ÷10; contrast with 0.004 to show what ÷100 would look like.
errorPatterns.distractor: The 4 in 0.04 is one hundredth of the other.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child knows it is smaller and moved one place, but names ÷100 or ÷2.

responseLevels.gap: Compares by the digit or by decimal length; cannot say one value is a tenth of the other.
responseLevels.full: States the ten-times / one-tenth relationship between adjacent places, justifies it by positional value, and applies it in both directions and across several places (e.g. 6,000 vs 0.006).
responseLevels.partial: States the 0.04 four is smaller and can order them, but cannot justify the exact ÷10 relationship or muddles the factor.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Look at the 4 in 0.4 and the 4 in 0.04. How do their values compare, and why?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands positional value says one is a tenth of the other and can say why (the place, not the digit, carries the value). A child stuck on face value says 'same, both are 4'; a child with the longer-is-larger error says the 0.04 one is bigger. The REASON separates true place-value understanding from a memorised comparison.
